claim: Place cell and grid cell representations are similar between rodents and bats.
source: The similarity in the place cell and, most remarkably, in the grid cell representation between rodents and bats suggests a common neural substrate for spatial navigation, shared across these mammals (Andersen and Buneo, 2002; Jacobs et al., 2010; Sereno and Lehky, 2011; Killian et al., 2012; Indovina et al., 2013; Jacobs et al., 2013; Thurley et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies comparing spatial representations across species.

claim: The similarity in spatial representations between rodents and bats suggests a common neural substrate for spatial navigation shared across mammals.
source: The similarity in the place cell and, most remarkably, in the grid cell representation between rodents and bats suggests a common neural substrate for spatial navigation, shared across these mammals (Andersen and Buneo, 2002; Jacobs et al., 2010; Sereno and Lehky, 2011; Killian et al., 2012; Indovina et al., 2013; Jacobs et al., 2013; Thurley et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observed similarity in spatial representations, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Place cells have been shown to directly generalize to three dimensions.
source: While place cell and head direction cells have been shown to directly generalize to three dimensions (Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013; Finkelstein et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Head direction cells have been shown to directly generalize to three dimensions.
source: While place cell and head direction cells have been shown to directly generalize to three dimensions (Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013; Finkelstein et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The form that grid cells will exhibit in higher dimensionality is still not clear.
source: the form that grid cells will exhibit in higher dimensionality (currently tested in flying bats [Ginosar et al., 2014]) is still not clear
evidence: The claim states the current state of knowledge in the field, with a citation to ongoing research.

claim: The question is still open of how the mechanism producing periodic patterns on a surface can extend to a volume in bats.
source: Further, the question is still open of how the mechanism producing such a complex periodic pattern on a surface can, in the case of bats, extend to a volume (Jeffery et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim identifies an open research question, supported by a citation.

claim: A regular lattice is information-theoretically optimal for spatial representation.
source: even when accepting the information-theoretic optimality of a regular lattice (Mathis et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a theoretical study.

claim: In the self-organization model, spatial responses emerge spontaneously at the single unit level with no engineering required.
source: In the self-organization perspective that we propose, the spatial responses first emerge spontaneously, at the single unit level, with no engineering required.
evidence: The claim describes a key feature of the authors' model.

claim: The periodicity of the grid pattern is a result of firing rate adaptation during exploration sessions that span a considerable developmental time.
source: In the simplest version of the model, which we have explored in a series of studies (Kropff and Treves, 2008; Si et al., 2012; Stella et al., 2013), the periodicity of the grid pattern is a result of firing rate adaptation during exploration sessions that span a considerable developmental time (Figure 1, c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and reference to Figure 1c showing the evolution of firing rate maps.

claim: The grid pattern is fixated gradually by means of synaptic plasticity in the feed-forward connections.
source: It is fixated gradually by means of synaptic plasticity in the feed-forward connections, which convey broad spatial inputs, for example but not necessarily from 'place units' (Figure 1, b).
evidence: The claim describes a mechanism in the model, with reference to Figure 1b showing the network architecture.

claim: The model can account for the effects of the geometry of the explored environment on the outcome of the self-organization process.
source: Contrary to other models limited to the explanation of grid cell expression, this model delves into the issue of their induction and, most importantly, can account for the effects of the geometry of the explored environment on the outcome of the self-organization process.
evidence: The claim describes a capability of the model.

claim: The model produces pentagonal grids on a spherical surface.
source: We have shown how, for example, the model produces pentagonal grids on a spherical surface and heptagonal ones on a hyperbolic one (Urdapilleta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The model produces heptagonal grids on a hyperbolic surface.
source: We have shown how, for example, the model produces pentagonal grids on a spherical surface and heptagonal ones on a hyperbolic one (Urdapilleta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The input network contains 123 units representing the CA1 region of the hippocampus.
source: The input network represents, for example, the CA1 region of the hippocampus and contains Ninp = 123 units.
evidence: The claim describes a parameter of the simulation model.

claim: The output network contains 125 would-be grid units in mEC.
source: The output network represents a population of NmEC = 125 would-be grid units in mEC, all with the same adaptation parameters when not differently stated.
evidence: The claim describes a parameter of the simulation model.

claim: Place cells develop an adult-like spatial code earlier than grid cells do.
source: Moreover, as recent studies have shown (Langston et al., 2010; Wills et al., 2010), it is entirely plausible that place cells develop an adult-like spatial code earlier than grid cells do.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Place field centers are homogeneously distributed in the volume.
source: Place field centers are homogeneously distributed in the volume (consistently with the experimental data presented in [Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013]).
evidence: The claim describes a model parameter that is consistent with experimental data cited.

claim: The choice of the value for the parameter σp is not itself crucial for the model.
source: Note that the choice of the value for the parameter σp is not itself crucial for our model (Kropff and Treves, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The properties of the developing grid fields depend on the time scale of adaptation and not on the size of the place fields.
source: As we show in the following, the properties of the developing grid fields depend on the time scale of adaptation and not on the size of the place fields.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model results presented in the paper.

claim: Three-dimensional space admits a multitude of equally optimal orderings of spheres.
source: Unlike on the plane, where the hexagonal tiling is always the optimal one, three-dimensional space admits a multitude of equally optimal orderings of spheres.
evidence: The claim is based on established mathematical knowledge about sphere packing.

claim: Face centered cubic (FCC) and hexagonal close packed (HCP) represent the only two regular solutions to the sphere packing problem.
source: The problem of sphere packing, in a volume of 3D space, is a well-known mathematical problem, and it is known since the time of Gauss that any of these infinite optimal solutions can be described in terms of two fundamental arrangements, called face centered cubic (FCC) and hexagonal close packed (HCP), that represent the only two regular solutions to the problem.
evidence: The claim is based on established mathematical knowledge attributed to Gauss.

claim: Both FCC and HCP solutions are based on a series of layers of spheres arranged in a hexagonal pattern.
source: Both solutions are based on a series of layers of spheres arranged in a hexagonal pattern.
evidence: The claim describes a mathematical property of FCC and HCP structures.

claim: In both FCC and HCP combinations, each sphere has 12 first neighbors.
source: In both combinations each sphere has 12 first neighbors
evidence: The claim describes a mathematical property of FCC and HCP structures.

claim: FCC and HCP differ only regarding the position of three spheres in the unit cell of 13 spheres.
source: If we consider the unit cell of 13 spheres (a central sphere + 12 neighbors) in Figure 2, then FCC and HCP differ only regarding the position of three spheres (compare the position of the fields marked in green and red in the top-left and top-right panels in Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 showing the structural differences.

claim: In FCC, neighbor spheres are arranged in six pairs with symmetrical positions with respect to the center.
source: In fact, while in FCC neighbor spheres are arranged in six pairs with symmetrical positions with respect to the center
evidence: The claim describes a mathematical property of FCC structure, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: In HCP, there are only three pairs of symmetrically positioned spheres, those on the central plane.
source: in HCP there are only three of these pairs, those on the central plane (fields marked in blue in Figure 2, top right).
evidence: The claim describes a mathematical property of HCP structure, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: For low values of γ parameter, the trivial solution ψ = 0 is favored in the cost function.
source: For small values of the parameter γ, instead, the trivial solution ψ = 0 is favored.
evidence: The claim is derived from analytical calculations of the cost function shown in Figure 5.

claim: As the value of γ parameter increases, solutions of higher power become successively favored for both FCC and HCP.
source: First of all, considering FCC and HCP separately, we see how, for both of them, solutions of higher power become successively favored as the value of the γ parameter increases, that is, as the weight of the adaptation component becomes increasingly dominant in the evaluation of the cost function.
evidence: The claim is derived from analytical calculations shown in Figure 5.

claim: FCC and HCP configurations alternate as the optimal solution in different portions of the parameter space.
source: In parallel, the two configurations, FCC and HCP, compete with each other, and the two are alternating as the optimal solution in different portions of the parameter space.
evidence: The claim is derived from analytical calculations shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is no evidence of a regime in which FCC strongly dominates HCP or vice versa.
source: There is no evidence of a regime in which one of the two strongly dominates the other.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the analytical calculations.

claim: The hexagonal arrangement and 12 first neighbors are the relevant features for the evaluation of the cost function.
source: Instead, the features that are common to the two, like the hexagonal arrangement and the 12 first neighbors, appear to be the relevant ones for the evaluation of the cost function
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the analytical results.

claim: The system does not appear to converge asymptotically to either FCC or HCP regular configurations of fields.
source: The system does not appear to converge asymptotically to either of the two regular configurations of fields.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from simulation results.

claim: Self-organized grids appear to express a mixture of symmetries.
source: Self-organized grids appear to express a mixture of symmetries
evidence: This is the title of a results section describing simulation outcomes.

claim: Starting from an initial random arrangement of connections, the combined effect of adaptation and synaptic learning leads units to approach a stable configuration.
source: Starting from an initial random arrangement of connections and a correspondingly heterogeneous distribution of activity, the combined effect of adaptation and synaptic learning leads the units to approach, after a transient reorganization of their firing fields in space, a stable configuration that is the outcome of the self-organization process.
evidence: The claim describes the general behavior of the model in simulations.

claim: After about 15 million time steps of learning time, firing rates of units present a blobby appearance with equally sized, spherical fields homogeneously distributed in the volume.
source: In Figure 4 we show two typical examples from the units emerging in the model mEC layer in two distinct simulations, each taken after about 15 million time steps of learning time. On the top row the firing rates of the units presents a blobby appearance, with equally sized, spherical fields homogeneously distributed in the volume.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: One simulated unit presents an approximately FCC arrangement of fields.
source: One is in fact presenting an approximately FCC arrangement (Figure 4, left)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: One simulated unit is close to an HCP arrangement of fields.
source: while the other is close to an HCP one (Figure 4, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Self-organization based on synaptic adaptation can have multiple outcomes, leading to equivalently stable solutions.
source: Thus, self-organization based on synaptic adaptation can have multiple outcomes, leading to equivalently stable solutions.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results showing different units with different arrangements.

claim: Identical systems with the same network properties might approach different asymptotic states as an effect of random initial conditions.
source: Identical systems, with the same network properties and subject to the same evolution dynamics might approach different asymptotic states, just as an effect of the random initial conditions.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results.

claim: After 15 million time steps, both FCC and HCP arrangements are present within the same mEC population.
source: In Figure 5 we show the distribution of the two scores, again taken after a long learning time (15 million time steps), for units all belonging to the same mEC population. The values of the two scores indicate the presence of both arrangements in the system.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Unit scores cover an entire continuum between pure FCC and pure HCP arrangements, expressing all intermediate arrangements.
source: If we look at the scores for each unit at a given time (Figure 5, left), we indeed find that these are not clustered in two groups, each one expressing a homogeneous HCP or FCC arrangement, but instead they cover an entire continuum of scores between the two extremes, expressing all intermediate arrangements.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The results point to a high degree of independence of each unit.
source: This result points to a high degree of independence of each unit
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the distribution of scores shown in Figure 5.

claim: The system shows a rather weak preference for either FCC or HCP regular configurations of fields.
source: and at the same time to a rather weak preference of the system for either of the regular configurations of fields.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the distribution of scores shown in Figure 5.

claim: The analytical calculations show a substantial equivalence of FCC and HCP ordering.
source: Analytical results show a substantial equivalence of FCC and HCP ordering
evidence: The claim summarizes the results of the analytical model.

claim: The discrepancy between observed configurations and symmetric solutions is due to small deviations of the relative phases between fields of different layers from the optimal ones.
source: The discrepancy between the configurations observed and the symmetric solutions, however, is not due to the emergence of mixtures of the two (like for example in a ABABCAB ordering of the layers), but rather to small deviations of the relative phases between fields of different layers from the optimal ones.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from analysis of the simulation results.

claim: The mean angle among neighboring fields is close to π/3 from the very beginning of learning.
source: The mean angle among neighboring fields (calculated over all the triplets of all the cells of a simulated population) is close to π/3 from the very beginning of learning and the real effect of continuing exploration is the reduction of the variability over the course of about 4 million time steps.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The variability in the mean angle among neighboring fields is reduced over the course of about 4 million time steps.
source: The mean angle among neighboring fields (calculated over all the triplets of all the cells of a simulated population) is close to π/3 from the very beginning of learning and the real effect of continuing exploration is the reduction of the variability over the course of about 4 million time steps.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mean spacing of the grids stabilizes after around 3-4 million time steps.
source: A similar behavior is observed when plotting the value of the mean spacing of the grids in time (calculated from the unit autocorrelograms) (Figure 6, right: blue line). Also in this case, after a short transient the value stabilizes after around 3–4 million time steps.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The model parameters lead to a spacing of 0.55 × L.
source: Our choice of model parameters (and specifically of the adaptation parameter) leads to a spacing of 0.55 × L.
evidence: The claim is a result from the simulations.

claim: Removing collateral connections appears to have no effect on the time course of grid spacing development.
source: In both cases we see that the time course of the development of a common grid spacing is not affected by the modifications of the standard model. Stabilization is obtained in the same time interval and while removing collateral connections appears to have absolutely no effect
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Variability in the adaptation parameter results in a slightly different final value of the spacing (0.5 × L).
source: the variability in the adaptation parameter results in a slightly different final value of the spacing (0.5 × L).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The three-dimensional grid develops from the same ingredients as its lower dimensional equivalent.
source: These results indicate that the three-dimensional grid develops from the same ingredients of its lower dimensional equivalent.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Mean spacing and mean angle are quickly fixed over the entire network almost simultaneously.
source: Mean spacing and mean angle are quickly fixed over the entire network almost simultaneously and are the first recognizable signs of the emergence of an ordered structure from the initial random distribution of activity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The presence of an additional dimension does not affect the way in which fields are initially brought by adaptation to homogeneously and regularly cover the entire space.
source: The presence of an additional dimension does not affect the way in which fields are initially brought by adaptation to homogeneously and regularly cover the entire space.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from comparing 2D and 3D simulation results.

claim: After roughly 4 million time steps, the system is already arranged in a stable ordered manner with equilateral triangles among neighboring fields.
source: Plotting the average across units of this index, which reflects the decrease of the variance in the angles between triplets, already observed in Figure 6, we see again (Figure 7, top left), that after roughly 4 million time steps the system is already arranged in a stable ordered manner, with equilateral triangles among neighboring fields that dominate the activity pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The ordering of equilateral triangles can be generated by the system independently of higher order symmetries.
source: This ordering can be generated by the system independently of higher order symmetries, and it provides a first step for further arranging fields in more articulated structures.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The hexagonal pattern score steadily rises to reach a value of about 0.85 after 6 million time steps and then remains stable.
source: In Figure 7 (top right) we plot the time evolution of the average over the population of this score. Starting from very low values, indicative of a still unorganized ensemble of fields, the score steadily rises to reach a value of about 0.85 (out of a maximum of 1) after 6 million time steps and then remains stable over the rest of the simulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Collateral interaction tends to align in time the principal layer of different cells, defining a preferred orientation for the global structure of the grid.
source: We indeed see that collateral interaction tends to align in time the principal layer of different cells, defining a preferred orientation for the global structure of the grid.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The emergence of the common alignment of the layers takes about 12 million time steps of exploration time.
source: The emergence of the common alignment of the layers is slower than the formation of the layers themselves. It takes about 12 million time steps of exploration time to significantly reduce the dispersion of the angles
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: After 30 million time steps, both FCC and HCP scores are still close to 0.5, reflecting the presence in the population of a large distribution of values.
source: Their values are almost unchanged over the duration of the simulations and after 30 million time steps, a time largely exceeding that necessary for the other quantities to converge, both of them are still close to 0.5, which reflects the presence in the population of a large distribution of values.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The simulations distinguish a hierarchy in the time course leading to the formation of three-dimensional grids.
source: Our simulations are able to distinguish a hierarchy in the time course leading to the formation of three-dimensional grids.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Different levels of complexity appear in the arrangement of fields with different speed.
source: Different levels of complexity appear in the arrangement of fields with different speed.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Fast converging quantities like the formation of equilateral triangles and layers of fields with hexagonal symmetry appear first.
source: Fast converging quantities like the formation of equilateral triangles of fields and successively of layers of fields with hexagonal symmetry appear first, framing the activity of single units in the network.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Planes of fields are rotated to align them across the population on a slower time scale.
source: These initial structures are then modified on a slower time scale to obtain a global coordination among cells. Planes of fields are rotated to align them across the population
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Self-organization does not appear to affect the aspects of network activity related to perfect FCC or HCP tiling even after a very extended period of time.
source: If we exclude the very initial phase of network dynamics, self-organization does not appear to affect these aspects of network activity that therefore remain loosely determined even after a very extended period of time.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The emergence of equilateral triangles in 3D requires roughly a factor 2 more time than in 2D.
source: The emergence of equilateral triangles in 3D appears to require roughly a factor 2 more time than in 2D (Si et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous 2D simulation results cited.

claim: The time for self-organization lengthens only a little, and clearly sublinearly, with the volume flown by the virtual bat.
source: In fact, however, we find that the time for self-organization lengthens only a little, and clearly sublinearly, with the volume flown by the virtual bat.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from simulation results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The population-averaged data points for both kinetic and adaptation terms can be well fit by a sum of two exponentials plus a constant.
source: We find that the population-averaged data points for both terms can be well fit by a sum of two exponentials, plus a constant (Figure 8, inset)
evidence: The claim is supported by data fitting shown in Figure 8.

claim: The relaxation of the estimated cost function is mainly determined by the most rapid exponential terms and is virtually complete by 3-4 million time steps.
source: We can see from Figure 8 that the relaxation of this estimated cost function is mainly determined by the most rapid exponential terms, and is virtually complete by 3–4 million time steps, with a limited volume dependence.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The time evolution of the cost function measure for volumes of different size appears to be quite similar.
source: Consequently, apart from the slight prolongation of the initial transient, the time evolution of our measure for volumes of different size appears to be quite similar.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The time required for grid development depends only weakly on the number of fields that have to be arranged in the volume.
source: These results suggest that the time required for the complex dynamics of grid development depends only weakly on the number of fields that have to be arranged in a orderly manner in the volume.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the volume-dependence analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The initial relaxation occurs in a time that increases sublinearly with system size.
source: The initial relaxation, which accomplishes most of the rearrangement and probably centers on adjusting the angles between triplets of fields (cp. Figure 7, top left and Figure 8), occurs in a time that increases sublinearly with system size.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the volume-dependence analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: With time steps of Δt = 10 ms and bat velocity of v = 1 m/s, the small environment corresponds to a cubic room of size L = 2.5 m.
source: If we take time steps of size Δt = 10 ms and an average bat velocity of v = 1 m/s, the small environment used in most of our simulations will correspond to a cubic room of size L = 2.5 m.
evidence: The claim specifies parameter values used to relate simulation results to real-world scales.

claim: With the specified parameters, grids are formed with a field spacing of approximately 1.4 m.
source: Then, with this choice of parameters, grids are formed with a field spacing of 2.5 m × 0.55 ≈ 1.4 m
evidence: The claim is a calculation based on simulation results and specified parameters.

claim: 1 million simulation time steps correspond to nearly 3 hours.
source: The time scale of grid formation can be calculated considering that 1 million simulation time steps correspond to 10,000 s or nearly 3 hr.
evidence: The claim is a calculation based on specified parameters.

claim: The model predicts the presence of triplets of fields forming roughly equilateral triangles in approximately 10-12 hours of continuous flight.
source: Our model then predicts, in an environment the size of ours, the presence of (i) triplets of fields forming roughly equilateral triangles in ≈10–12 hr of continuous flight
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on simulation results and specified parameters.

claim: The model predicts hexagons in approximately 15-18 hours of continuous flight.
source: (ii) hexagons in ≈15–18 hr
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on simulation results and specified parameters.

claim: The model predicts different units achieve a common orientation after approximately 30-35 hours of continuous flight.
source: and finally (iii) different units that achieve a common orientation after ≈30–35 hr.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on simulation results and specified parameters.

claim: These time scales do not seem very different from those predicted by the same model for the development of grids in a two-dimensional environment of similar linear size.
source: These time scales do not seem very different from those predicted by the same model for the development of grids in a two-dimensional environment of similar linear size (relative to the grid spacing).
evidence: The claim is a comparison with previous 2D model results.

claim: The 2D model indicates a time scale of about 5-6 hours for the development of gridness.
source: Figure 6 in Si et al. (2012) indicates a time scale of about 20,000 s, or 5–6 hr, for the development of gridness in 2D.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The moderate increase in grid formation time might make it comparable to the flight time available for spatial learning during bat experiments.
source: At the same time, this moderate increase in grid formation time might make it comparable to the flight time available for spatial learning during bat experiments.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the implications of the model predictions.

claim: The weak, sub-linear dependence of time scales with volume may be sufficient to determine a switch between the possibility of forming regular structures and leaving them beyond reach.
source: In these conditions, even the weak, sub-linear dependence of time scales with volume, that we do observe, may be sufficient to determine a switch between the possibility of forming regular structures and leaving them beyond reach.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the implications of the model results.

claim: The total simulation time would correspond to a maximum of approximately 80-90 hours of continuous bat flight in the (2.5 m)³ volume.
source: The total simulation time would correspond to a maximum of ≈80–90 hr of continuous bat flight in the (2.5 m)3 volume.
evidence: The claim is a calculation based on simulation duration and specified parameters.

claim: 80-90 hours is just a lower bound for the time necessary to form a regular tiling of the environment, and likely a loose one.
source: This time is just a lower bound for the time necessary to form a regular tiling of the environment, and likely a loose one, as our simulations do not seem to be converging towards one of them.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Bats may form a partially regular 3D tiling of the environment at most once, and then possibly only if constrained to fly for a prolonged time in a rather small cage.
source: These considerations suggest that bats may form a partially regular 3D tiling of the environment at most once, and then possibly only if constrained to fly for a prolonged time in a rather small cage
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the model predictions and time scale analysis.

claim: A completely regular, crystalline tiling of space seems to be hardly in the range of time available to real bats.
source: while a completely regular, crystalline tiling of space seems to be hardly in the range of time available to real bats.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the model predictions and time scale analysis.

claim: The presence of an additional dimension does not seem to preclude the appearance of some orderly arrangement of the fields in mEC units of bats.
source: In conclusion, the presence of an additional dimension does not seem to preclude the appearance of some orderly arrangement of the fields in mEC units of bats.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The order in 3D grids might express only a partial set of the full spectrum of potential three-dimensional symmetry properties.
source: Nevertheless, this order might express only a partial set of the full spectrum of potential three-dimensional symmetry properties.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The partial order might be sufficient to distinguish the activity of these cells from a random multi-peaked pattern.
source: It might be still sufficient to distinguish the activity of these cells from a random multi-peaked pattern, but it would place it at a substantial distance from a perfectly regular pattern, too.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the implications of the model results.

claim: In the model, the distance from perfect symmetry varies across a population of cells, with some showing only small deviations from perfect symmetry.
source: In our model this distance varies across a population of cells: some of them show only small deviations from perfect symmetry.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The vast majority of simulated grid cells are very far from a perfectly regular arrangement.
source: At the same time, the vast majority of simulated grid cells are very far from a perfectly regular arrangement
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The bulk of grid-like but imperfect cells can be regarded as a robust aspect of the model.
source: the bulk of grid-like but imperfect cells can be regarded as a robust aspect of our model, and might extend to very different situations of 3D grid cell development, possibly including other species experiencing three-dimensional navigation.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the generalizability of the model results.
